builder_plan.scenario: Your coding assistant makes changes that still need substantial repair before merging.
builder_plan.change: Try the technique on held-out issues from a repository with reliable tests.
builder_plan.baseline: The same coding agent, repository snapshot, tools, and token budget.
steps: Locate the paper's implementation and check its license, model support, data needs, and hardware requirements. Stop here if you cannot obtain the required artifacts.
Save a small set of representative product tasks and expected outcomes. Keep evaluation tasks out of any training or tuning, and choose quality and cost limits before running.
Run the baseline and the proposed change on identical inputs. Keep other settings fixed and repeat paired runs to expose variation.
Save per-task outputs, failures, timings, and all usage costs. Review regressions before expanding the test.
builder_plan.measure: Correct patches, regression failures, human repair time, and total cost per accepted change.
builder_plan.decision: Keep the change only if it meets your preselected quality and latency limits and improves the metric you care about after setup and operating costs. Otherwise retain the baseline. This is an exploration plan, not a validated recommendation.

title: Termination Lag: Coding Agents Solve Early but Stop Late
summary: The paper is a measurement study, not a deployable method: it characterizes termination lag by testing every intermediate patch, which replaces nothing directly but motivates early-stopping or patch-checkpointing policies in place of fixed step budgets. Adopting an early-stop or best-patch-selection policy costs a per-step patch-evaluation harness (test execution per candidate patch) plus policy-tuning complexity. It can fail because stopping at the first test-passing patch risks accepting an incomplete or overfit solution, while continuing risks regressions in the 1-8% of runs where agents undo correct work.
rationale: The finding directly implies substantial wasted compute and occasional regressions in coding-agent runs, but no validated stopping rule is provided, so the reader should validate a cheap early-exit or best-checkpoint policy on their own workload before production use.

claims.statement: The paper is a measurement study, not a deployable method: it characterizes termination lag by testing every intermediate patch, which replaces nothing directly but motivates early-stopping or patch-checkpointing policies in place of fixed step budgets. Adopting an early-stop or best-patch-selection policy costs a per-step patch-evaluation harness (test execution per candidate patch) plus policy-tuning complexity. It can fail because stopping at the first test-passing patch risks accepting an incomplete or overfit solution, while continuing risks regressions in the 1-8% of runs where agents undo correct work.
Post-solution steps account for a median of 35-37% (Qwen3-Coder) and 54-60% (Laguna-XS.2) of successful runs; 1-8% of continued activity undoes a correct patch.
